p1_engine.eyebrow: A registry-confirmed claim, behind a genuinely uncertain identity

blocks.text: The single strongest fact in this entire profile is also the one most worth double-checking against the identity ambiguity: an Indian Patent Office patent-agent examination paper names 'Hindustan Pharmaceuticals' as a pioneer in alkaloid production in India — a registry-confirmed source, the strongest credibility tier this project uses, not a self-claim. But which 'Hindustan Pharmaceuticals' the exam paper refers to was not independently re-confirmed this session.

The company's own listed website (hindustanpharmaceuticals.com) is an expired, parked domain now for sale — meaning even a direct check of 'the company's own claims' isn't currently possible through the channel the HVT sheet points to.

This session's research instead found a plausible candidate: a herbal-extract exporter based in Amritsar, Punjab (hindphrm.com), founded in 1971 by Raman Gupta, exporting medicinal herbs and herbal extracts since 1995 — consistent with the HVT sheet's 'herbal-extracts-medicines' sector and segment classification, but not confirmed as the same legal entity the patent-office source or the HVT sheet's own notes field describes.

The HVT sheet's own notes field independently documents the identity problem: GST registrations exist for a proprietorship (named owner: Sanjeev Kumar) and, separately, a partnership entity under a similar name — the HVT tool itself could not cleanly resolve which entity its own pillar research describes.

It claims to hold WHO-GMP/WHO-CGMP, TUV Nord ISO 9001 and USFDA site registration, and to have patented a drug 'important for public health in India' — both self-claimed via a third-party directory (chemdmart.com), and the HVT sheet flags both `moat` and `product_improvement` `needs_verify: yes`.

insights.point: The field is **large and growing very fast**, with India specifically outpacing the global rate.
insights.evidence: Global herbal medicine market: $100-251B (2024-25) to $396-516B by 2034-35 depending on methodology; India's own herbal medicine market is growing faster still, $7.26B (2025) to $30.0B by 2035, ~15.2%/yr.

insights.point: **Export demand is real and geographically concentrated**, matching where a genuine herbal exporter would want to be.
insights.evidence: India's Ayush exports doubled over the past decade to $2.16B across 150 countries; the US alone absorbed 34.95% of Ayush exports, with raw herbs and extracts making up 60-70% of export volume — a category the candidate Amritsar entity's own 1995-onward export history fits.

insights.point: Named peers in this category are **all substantially larger** — no scale-comparable peer was found.
insights.evidence: Dabur India (₹12,404 Cr revenue), Himalaya Wellness (~$440M), Shree Baidyanath (₹761 Cr) all operate at a scale many multiples above what a small sole-proprietorship exporter would show — useful as market-structure context, not a benchmark.

reflect.text: A registry-confirmed pioneer claim sitting inside a name and legal-entity picture this research genuinely could not pin down. The market opportunity is real regardless; which specific company gets credit for the patent-office claim is the thing to resolve first.
